newsitem.title: MEXICO: Elections in Mexico may rush debt issues -analysts.
newsitem.headline: Elections in Mexico may rush debt issues -analysts.

text.p: Mexico could rush to capital markets again early this year to take advantage of a calm before what are expected to be stormy mid-year elections that could cool investor sentiment, analysts said on Wednesday.

The long-ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) faces tough challenges to its control of the lower house of Congress and the office of mayor of Mexico City in the July 7 polls. Moreover, there will be races for several governorships and municipal presidents this year.
Mexico's first move this year was made on Wednesday, when it launched a $1.0 billion, 10-year fixed rate global bond at 337.5 basis points over U.S. Treasuries.
Mexico is also taking advantage of good international liquidity and low U.S. interest rates, analysts said.

"They have to take advantage of the conditions to obtain the yields they want. If things continue to be quiet, that is good, but really there is a preoccupation that the elections will cause a lot of noise," said Santander Investments economist Hector Chavez.
The perception that the elections will cause at least short-term market turmoil is widespread in the investment community.

Some market players worry that hardliners within the PRI will struggle to keep power at any cost and that those attempts to hold onto power could put pressure on Mexico's monetary and fiscal policies.

On Wednesday, Bear Stearns & Co issued a report that said political developments in Mexico this year could create significant volatility for Mexican securities, despite what it called a disciplined macroeconomic strategy and a highly pro-active and creative liability-management strategy.
"On the whole, these factors argue in favor of maintaining a neutral position in Mexican sovereign debt," Bear Stearns wrote.
The federal government -- the United Mexican States -- only has $1.4 billion coming due this year, and its new global bond issue is seen covering a good part of that debt.
"It is part of the plan of Mexico to refinance its maturing debt this year," Merrill Lynch economist Pablo Riveroll said.
But there are a number of other government agencies that have to refinance maturing debt this year, such as oil giant Petroleos Mexicanos and the Federal Electricity Commission.
In total, Mexican government borrowers will need to refinance $4.047 billion of debt in the international capital markets in 1997.
Mexico also has a heavy schedule of maturing debt in the next few years to pay back what it owes to the U.S. Treasury and the International Monetary Fund.
"During the year they will surely (go to the market again), but we cannot say at what conditions," Riveroll said.
Mexican corporate borrowers could also take advantage of the good conditions to go to markets soon, analysts said.
